contract: Append-only, like the domain-relevance benchmark. Every case carries the verdict observed against the analyzer named in frozenAgainst, so a later reader can tell a fixed defect from a moved goalpost. `expected` is the adjudicated target behavior; `observedAtFreeze` is what the shipped analyzer actually did when the case was written down. A case whose expected and observedAtFreeze disagree is RED on purpose.

misreadingPolarity.question: When a source's wording overlaps an indexed commonMisreading, does the analyzer say the right thing about who is claiming what?
misreadingPolarity.ruling: Strong misreading-surface overlap is Contradicts by default: the canon indexes that reading as one it explicitly rejects, so a source asserting it disagrees with the canon. Local negation means the source is stating the canon's own correction and reads Supports. Quotation or attribution means the source is reporting someone else's claim, not making one, and is downgraded to report-handling rather than being credited to the speaker.

cases.text: Passing every listed factor creates attraction and entitlement to a relationship.
cases.note: Confirmed case from the v2.4.0 brief. The canon's commonMisreading for hierarchy:overview is literally 'Passing a person's listed factors does not create attraction, consent, compatibility, or entitlement to a relationship.' The source asserts the thing the canon denies and the analyzer calls it a resemblance.

cases.text: A large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates.
cases.note: Confirmed case from the v2.4.0 brief. Highest-scoring of the three: the overlap is with title, alias AND commonMisreading surfaces.

cases.text: Message concentration proves the same minority monopolizes relationships.
cases.note: Confirmed case from the v2.4.0 brief, and the purest of the three: EVERY shared token comes from the commonMisreading surface and nothing else. If misreading-surface provenance cannot fix this one, it cannot fix any of them.

cases.text: It is false that a large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates.
cases.note: Exactly inverted today. The source agrees with the canon and is labelled as contradicting it, because the current rule reads the word 'false' as disagreement with the MATCH rather than with the misreading.

cases.text: A large inbox is not a large pool of relationship candidates.
cases.note: Same sentence as mp-02 plus one 'not', and today it scores identically and is labelled identically. Bare 'is not' is absent from the contradiction cue list, so the analyzer cannot currently tell mp-02 and mp-05 apart at all.

cases.text: Message concentration does not prove that the same minority monopolizes relationships.
cases.note: Inverted. This sentence is close to a verbatim restatement of the canon's own boundary.

cases.text: Passing every listed factor does not create attraction or entitlement to a relationship.
cases.note: The sharpest illustration of the inversion: this is a near-verbatim paraphrase of the canon's own commonMisreading correction, and the analyzer files it as a contradiction of the canon at High confidence.

cases.text: Some men claim that a large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates.
cases.note: The speaker is reporting a claim, not making it. Report-handling: the misreading must not be attributed to this passage's author.

cases.text: According to the podcast, message concentration proves the same minority monopolizes relationships.
cases.note: The worst of the attribution cases: 'According to' trips the evidence cue, so the analyzer reports that the source SUPPORTS the canon while the source is in fact relaying the canon's own indexed misreading.

cases.text: He kept insisting that passing every listed factor creates attraction and entitlement to a relationship.
cases.note: Third-party attribution without a reporting cue in the contradiction or evidence lists.

candidateRetention.question: When an exact phrase, exact alias, or concept-signature hit is detected, does it survive to adjudication, or is it truncated out of the candidate set first?
candidateRetention.ruling: The working candidate set is the union of the top-scored candidates and every evidence-bearing hit. Retention is not credibility: a retained hit still has to earn admission on its own score and evidence. Ranking and display caps apply after the union, not before it.

cases.text: She wanted a provider who could support a household while she raised their children.
cases.note: The case named in the v2.4.0 brief, reproduced to the decimal (0.452 / 0.372 / vanished). Also benchmark case ds-07 verbatim, which the domain-gate append added specifically so the ratified `provider` alias could be tested. The alias fires, scores 0.30, is cut to 0.156 by the sparse-shared-token penalty, ranks 12th, and is discarded by the 8-candidate cap before anything can look at it.

cases.text: Across Latin America the provider role is still the default expectation for men in dating, and women report that a partner's earnings and stability matter to whether the relationship lasts.
cases.note: The same loss with no sparse penalty: the alias holds its full 0.30 and is still discarded, purely because eight other entries out-rank it on generic overlap. This is the retention defect isolated from the scoring one.

cases.text: The provider role is still the default expectation for men in dating, and women across regions and income levels report that a partner's earnings and stability matter to whether the relationship lasts.
cases.note: Lost by one rank. 141 entries clear the candidate floor on this passage and the only one carrying an exact alias hit is the one that gets cut.

cases.text: She wanted a breadwinner who could carry the household while she raised their children.
cases.note: Second ratified alias on the same entry, same fate. Only eleven entries clear the floor at all and the exact-alias hit still does not make the cut.

candidateRetention.property: Beyond the named cases, the union contract is asserted as a property over every case in this block: no entry carrying an exact phrase hit, an exact alias hit, or a concept-signature hit may be absent from the working candidate set while a lower-evidence entry is present in it.

typedAlias.question: Can a single curated word ever be sufficient evidence, and if so which words and under what conditions?
typedAlias.ruling: A single word is insufficient by default. A curated high-specificity alias, or a contextual alias with independent relational evidence, may be sufficient.

cases.text: Hypergamy shapes modern dating.
cases.note: Named in the v2.4.0 brief. The passage is gated `relevant`, the alias fires exactly, and the match still fails admission because a single-word alias is worth 0.30 against a 0.43 floor. The evidence is found and then thrown away.

cases.text: Hypergamy is the reason she kept dating men who out-earned her.
cases.note: The same alias in a longer passage: it holds its full 0.30 and drops to 14th of 58 because generic dating vocabulary outranks the one term that actually names the concept.

cases.text: She wanted a provider who could support a household while she raised their children.
cases.note: Benchmark case ds-07 verbatim. Participant and relationship-outcome frames both fire independently of the word `provider`, which is exactly the co-fire the contextual class asks for.

cases.text: Across Latin America the provider role is still the default expectation for men in dating, and women report that a partner's earnings and stability matter to whether the relationship lasts.
She wanted a breadwinner who could carry the household while she raised their children.

cases.trap: healthcare provider
cases.text: Her insurance changed and she had to find a new healthcare provider this year.

cases.trap: cloud provider
cases.text: We migrated the app to a different cloud provider last quarter.

cases.trap: internet service provider
cases.text: My internet service provider throttles the connection every evening.

cases.trap: cloud provider, surviving the domain gate
cases.text: My girlfriend and I spent the whole weekend arguing about which cloud provider our startup should use.
cases.note: The hard negative, and the one that decides whether the contextual class is safe. ta-06 to ta-08 are rejected by the domain gate before the alias is ever consulted, so they prove nothing about alias typing. This one is retained `uncertain` with both a participant frame and a relationship-outcome frame firing, so the co-fire condition alone is satisfied and only the alias's own local collocation separates it from ta-03.

cases.trap: sports game
cases.text: The game went into overtime and the crowd would not sit down.

cases.trap: video game
cases.text: He stayed up all night grinding the same game on his console.

cases.trap: video game, surviving the domain gate
cases.text: The studio patched the game so ranked players get fewer unfair matches.
cases.note: Benchmark case ds-13 verbatim, already recorded there as a KNOWN MISS: the append-1 dating-app-interaction mechanism frame retains it fail-open on 'fewer ... matches'. It is repeated here because that fail-open retention is precisely what would expose smv:charm's `game` alias to a video-game passage if `game` were typed contextual.

cases.trap: rizz as generic praise
cases.text: That new sneaker colorway has rizz, easily the best drop of the year.
cases.note: Benchmark case ds-15 verbatim.

contextualCoFire.question: When a contextual alias fires, is the relational evidence that promotes it near THAT occurrence, or merely somewhere in the passage?
contextualCoFire.ruling: Contextual promotion is occurrence-local. Each occurrence of a contextual alias earns or fails promotion on evidence inside a bounded window around itself, clipped to its own clause; relational vocabulary elsewhere in the passage does not reach it, and one disqualified occurrence does not suppress a legitimate one. The technical-modifier denylist is a secondary defense and is token-bounded, so hyphens and compounds cannot slip past it. Vendor names are not enumerated: they fail because the window test finds no relational evidence, which is the rule that generalizes.
contextualCoFire.provenance: Sol verification review of v2.4.0 + v2.4.1, section 1 CONTEST. cf-01 and cf-02 are Sol's repro table verbatim and reproduce to the decimal (0.540 credible, both). cf-03 through cf-06 are adversarial extensions written for this pass.

cases.trap: unlisted vendor name, relational noun far from the occurrence
cases.text: My girlfriend and I spent the whole weekend arguing about which AWS provider our startup should use.
cases.note: Sol's repro, verbatim. `AWS` is not on the notAfter denylist and never will be — enumerating vendors is not a rule. The promotion is carried by the outcome frame firing on `arguing`, which belongs to a different clause than the alias. `girlfriend` sits eleven tokens away and is about the arguing, not the provider.

cases.trap: hyphenated compound defeats the literal denylist string
cases.text: My girlfriend and I spent the whole weekend arguing about which cloud-based provider our startup should use.
cases.note: Sol's repro, verbatim. `cloud` IS on the denylist; the check is `normalized.includes('cloud provider')`, so the hyphen in `cloud-based` defeats it. Same sentence as ta-09, which passes only because it says `cloud provider` with a literal space. This is the case that proves the denylist must be token-bounded rather than a substring test.

cases.trap: one technical occurrence and one legitimate occurrence in the same passage
cases.text: We switched to a different cloud provider last quarter, and throughout their marriage he was still the only provider for his wife and children.
cases.note: The occurrence-independence case. The passage clears the domain gate (`explicit-relational-outcome`), and the second `provider` is as relational as ta-03's. It maps to nothing, because `promotedAliases` finds the literal string `cloud provider` anywhere in the passage and `continue`s past the alias entirely — one disqualified occurrence suppresses every occurrence. The expected occurrence accounting requires per-occurrence fields the analyzer does not yet publish, so that half of the assertion is RED by construction.

cases.trap: two vendor occurrences, neither relational, no relational noun anywhere
cases.text: The team argued for hours about whether the Azure provider or the Oracle provider had better uptime.
cases.note: Adversarial extension. Strips cf-01's `girlfriend` so the only thing carrying promotion is the outcome frame on `argued`. The passage contains no relational vocabulary at all and still promotes, which shows the defect is the passage-global frame test rather than any particular noun.

cases.trap: decisive relational outcome in a different clause from the occurrence
cases.text: Marriage rates came up briefly at dinner, but the argument was really about which billing provider our startup should integrate.
cases.note: Adversarial extension, and the cleanest statement of the window rule. `Marriage` is a decisive relational outcome, so the passage is correctly gated relevant — but it is in the first clause and the alias is in the second, and `billing` is not on the denylist. Passage-global co-fire cannot tell this apart from a real provisioning claim; a clause-clipped window can.

cases.trap: legitimate occurrence whose relational evidence must survive the tightening
cases.text: For most of that marriage he was the provider and she managed everything else at home.
cases.note: Adversarial extension, GREEN at freeze and included as a guard rather than a repro. Its relational evidence (`marriage`) sits four tokens from the alias in the same clause, so it must survive occurrence-local scoping. Paired with cf-05, which has the same word in the same sentence but out of reach: the two differ only in where the evidence sits, which is exactly the discrimination this block is about.

stanceComposition.question: When a passage overlaps an indexed commonMisreading, does the stance label survive negation scope, quotation, attribution, endorsement, rejection, and qualification — including when they compose?
stanceComposition.ruling: Stance is clause-scoped. A negator binds the clause it sits in and the complement it governs, not the whole sentence, and negators compose by parity rather than by presence. A quoted span reports the misreading only when the span carries the assertion itself; a quote around a bare noun phrase inside the speaker's own sentence does not make the speaker a reporter. Attribution hands the claim to someone else, but a following clause that endorses it hands it back, and one that rejects it makes the speaker a denier. A following clause that qualifies the claim breaks the asserted/denied binary and reads Challenges. Irony is not detected and is not claimed to be — see sc-07.
stanceComposition.provenance: Sol verification review of v2.4.0 + v2.4.1, section 2 CONTEST. sc-01 through sc-07 are Sol's table verbatim and reproduce to the decimal. sc-08 through sc-12 are composition variants written for this pass. Every case in this block uses the same indexed misreading, so the only variable is the wrapper.
stanceComposition.misreading: a large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates

cases.text: It is not false that a large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates.
cases.note: Sol's table, verbatim. `MISREADING_DENIAL_CUES` is a presence test, so two negators read the same as one: `not` and `false` each match, the sentence is called a denial, and a double negative that asserts the misreading is filed as agreeing with the canon. Parity, not presence.

cases.text: The editor printed 'a large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates' in scare quotes.
cases.note: Sol's table, verbatim. The v2.4.0 ruling covers 'quotation or attribution', but quotation marks are never actually detected — `REPORTED_SPEECH_CUES` is a verb list, and `printed` is not on it. The whole misreading sits inside quotes and the analyzer charges it to the editor's newspaper as if the passage asserted it.

cases.text: A large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates, but that equivalence is overstated.
cases.note: Sol's table, verbatim. The source asserts the equivalence and then withdraws part of it. Forced through an asserted/denied binary this can only come out as full assertion, which overstates the disagreement. Qualification is a third thing and the label for it already exists.

cases.text: The podcast says a large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates, and that is exactly right.
cases.note: Sol's table, verbatim. Attribution is detected and stops there. The speaker relays the misreading and then adopts it in the next clause, which makes it the speaker's own claim; filing it as Context only records no disagreement where there plainly is one.

cases.text: He says a large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates, but he is wrong.
cases.note: Sol's table, verbatim. The mirror of sc-04. The speaker relays the misreading and rejects it, which is the canon's own correction stated out loud, and the analyzer records nothing. Note `denial: true` at freeze — the sentence-global cue did fire on `wrong`, and was simply outranked by the reported-speech branch.

cases.text: A large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates, not a guarantee of marriage.
cases.note: Sol's table, verbatim. The `not` negates `a guarantee of marriage` in a trailing clause; the pool equivalence in front of the comma is asserted flatly. A sentence-global cue cannot see the comma, so the passage is credited with stating the canon's limit when it is stating the misreading and then narrowing a different thing.

cases.text: Sure, a large inbox is a 'large pool of relationship candidates'—and every spam message is a soulmate.
cases.note: STATED INSTRUMENT LIMIT, not a defect, and the one case in Sol's table this pass does not fix. The speaker is sarcastically rejecting the misreading, so the humanly correct label is Supports; the analyzer says Contradicts and will continue to. Detecting irony needs world knowledge the local deterministic stack does not have and cannot fake. Frozen asserting CURRENT behavior so that the clause-scoped rewrite is held to preserving it: the quoted span here covers a bare noun phrase inside the speaker's own sentence, and must NOT be read as reported speech the way sc-02's full quoted clause is. Published in the lab.html instrument-limits section.

cases.text: He says it is not true that a large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates.
cases.note: Composition variant, GREEN at freeze and included as a guard. The speaker reports someone else denying the misreading and takes no position of their own, so the standing doctrine applies unchanged: a reported claim carries no stance to record, whichever way the reported claim points. It is here because the rewrite makes negation and attribution interact, and this is the composition that must NOT change.

cases.text: The podcast says a large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates, though that equivalence is overstated.
cases.note: Composition variant. sc-03's qualification applied to sc-04's attribution. The speaker relays the claim and then qualifies it, which is a stance of the speaker's own — a partial rejection — so attribution does not get to end the analysis.

cases.text: She wrote, "the article said 'a large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates' outright."
cases.note: Composition variant, GREEN at freeze and included as a guard. Two levels of reporting and no endorsement or rejection at either level, so it stays Context only. It is here because quoted-span detection is new in this pass and must not double-count nesting into some other label.

cases.text: He says a large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates, but that is false.
cases.note: Composition variant, and sc-05 with the rejection worded impersonally rather than as `he is wrong`. Included so the fix cannot be a special case for one phrasing.

cases.text: A large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates, but that is false.
cases.note: Composition variant, GREEN at freeze — for the wrong reason, which is why it is frozen. The sentence-global denial cue happens to fire on `false` and lands on the right label by accident. After the rewrite the same label must be reached deliberately: the assertion clause has parity zero, and the following clause rejects it. A guard against fixing sc-06 by simply deleting trailing-clause sensitivity.

clauseMechanics.question: Which of Sol's v2.5.0 stance and co-fire failures are implementation bugs rather than gaps in what a punctuation-based clause model can represent at all?
clauseMechanics.ruling: Five, and only five. Each of these is a rule the release already claimed to have, applied to a case the code does not actually reach: a dash the normalizer disguised as a hyphen, a denylist that only looks backwards, a one-follow-up rule that scans every following clause, a reported-speech branch that can only see a comment if punctuation created a clause to hold it, and an interrogative inversion counted as a denial. Everything else in the review is a limit of the model, is frozen as one in the block below this, and is NOT attempted here — a cue list grown to cover cases nobody adjudicated is how cue lists rot.
clauseMechanics.misreading: a large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates

cases.trap: no-space em dash reads as an intra-word hyphen
cases.text: We discussed our marriage—the AWS provider failed again.

observedAtFreeze.promotedBy: relational role term “marriage” within 8 tokens, same clause

cases.note: Sol's repro, verbatim. `normalizeText` folds an em dash to an ASCII hyphen, which is right for matching and wrong for splitting: `marriage—the` becomes `marriage-the`, and the splitter's own rule — a hyphen ends a clause only when it is not joining two word characters — then keeps two independent claims inside one clause. The occurrence-local window works exactly as designed on a clause that should not exist.

cases.trap: technical sense established AFTER the alias
cases.text: During our marriage the provider for cloud hosting handled our archive.

observedAtFreeze.promotedBy: relational role term “marriage” within 8 tokens, same clause

cases.note: Sol's repro, verbatim. `cloud` and `hosting` are both on this alias's denylist and both sit AFTER the occurrence, where `disqualifyingModifier` never looks. English puts a noun's complement after it at least as often as its modifier before it, so a backwards-only denylist can be defeated by word order alone.

cases.trap: post-nominal complement, plural denylist term
cases.text: During our marriage the provider of payroll services handled our archive.
cases.note: Sol's second illustration of the same defect. `service` is on the denylist and `services` is the word actually written, so this case also fixes the singular-only matching the lookback has always had. `payroll` is on no list and never needs to be — the complement is disqualifying because a listed term is inside it.

cases.trap: post-nominal complement that is RELATIONAL
cases.text: During our marriage the provider for the household was always him.
cases.note: GUARD, green at freeze. The same shape as cm-02 with a relational complement instead of a technical one. Post-nominal detection that disqualified on the shape rather than on the denylist would break this, and `provider for the household` is the most ordinary phrasing this entry has.

cases.wrapper: attribution + rejection across a no-space em dash
cases.text: He says a large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates—but he is wrong.
cases.note: Sol's repro, verbatim, and the same root cause as cm-01 on the other feature — which is the argument for fixing it in the splitter both of them share. `wrong` is counted as a negator inside the assertion clause and then discarded by the reported branch, so the sentence reads as a bare relay. cm-06 is the identical sentence with a semicolon and it is already right.

cases.text: He says a large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates; but he is wrong.
cases.note: GUARD, green at freeze. The pair cm-05/cm-06 is what makes the diagnosis a diagnosis: same words, same claim, same verdict owed, and the only difference is which mark the writer typed.

cases.wrapper: attribution + endorsement two clauses away, about something else
cases.text: He says a large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates; the episode then discusses the weather; the forecast is exactly right.
cases.note: Sol's repro, verbatim. What is endorsed is the forecast. The v2.5.0 release states the rule as “exactly one follow-up, from clauses after the assertion”; the code scans every later clause until a cue fires, which is a different rule that happens to agree on the fixtures that were written.

cases.wrapper: attribution + rejection two clauses away, about something else
cases.text: He says a large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates; the episode then discusses the weather; the forecast is wrong.
cases.note: Sol's repro, verbatim. The mirror of cm-07, and the pair matters: a fix that only stopped endorsements from reaching across would leave the analyzer crediting the speaker with a correction they made about the weather.

cases.wrapper: attribution + rejection three clauses away, with an inert clause between
cases.text: He says a large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates; the study, however, is wrong.
cases.note: ACCEPTED COST, not a repro. The rejection here is genuinely about the reported claim, and the one-clause window loses it because a parenthetical `however` created two clause breaks between the assertion and the verdict. Recorded rather than discovered later: enforcing the stated rule costs this case, and the failure is to Context only, which under-claims rather than over-claims. Frozen as a documented limit in the block below.

cases.text: He says a large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates and he is exactly right.
cases.note: Sol's repro, verbatim. The speaker adopts the reported reading in the same breath. Follow-up handling can only see a comment that punctuation put in a later clause, so a coordinated one is invisible — and the whole point of the reported branch is that adopting a relayed claim makes it yours.

cases.text: He says a large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates and that is false.
cases.note: The mirror of cm-10, and the reason the fix is written as “a comment after the misreading's own span” rather than as an endorsement rule. Both directions or neither.

cases.wrapper: matrix denial BEFORE the misreading, one clause
cases.text: It is false that the following claim holds: a large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates.
cases.note: GUARD AND LIMIT. Sol's colon-governed denial: the humanly correct answer is Supports and the analyzer says Contradicts, because the colon severs the matrix `false` from the claim it governs. It is in THIS block, asserting current behavior, because the cm-10/cm-11 fix scans the assertion clause AFTER the misreading span, and a fix that scanned the whole clause instead would flip this case by accident — moving a limit while appearing to leave it alone.

cases.text: Is it not obvious that a large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates?
cases.note: Sol's repro, verbatim. `Is it not X?` asserts X. The negator belongs to the inversion, not to the proposition, and counting it flips a plain assertion of the misreading into a denial of it. No irony inference is required and none is being attempted — this is one fixed syntactic frame.

cases.text: Isn't it obvious that a large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates?
cases.note: The contracted form of cm-13, in the block so the fix cannot be a literal match on one spelling.

cases.wrapper: declarative control carrying the same negator
cases.text: It is not obvious that a large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates.
cases.note: GUARD, green at freeze, and the one that keeps the fix narrow. Same words as cm-13 minus the inversion and the question mark, and here the negator really does deny the claim. If this case moves, the fix has become a rule about the word `not` instead of a rule about one interrogative frame.

cases.trap: denylist term whose plural is not the literal term plus an s
cases.text: During our marriage the provider of utilities handled our archive.

observedAtFreeze.promotedBy: relational role term “marriage” within 8 tokens, same clause

cases.note: Sol's v2.6.1 repro, verbatim, and defect b again rather than a new one: the same complement branch cm-02 and cm-03 bought, defeated by morphology instead of by word order. `utility` is on the denylist and the comparison tests the literal term and a naive `${modifier}s`, so it asks whether the complement contains `utilitys` and never whether it contains `utilities`. The two sides of the comparison are not in the same representation, which is the actual defect; the missing word is only how it surfaced.

cases.trap: the same derived plural in the BACKWARD lookback rather than the complement
cases.text: During our marriage the utilities provider handled our archive.

observedAtFreeze.promotedBy: relational role term “marriage” within 8 tokens, same clause

cases.note: The same word in the oldest half of the rule. Both directions call one comparison helper, so a fix written only into the v2.6.0 complement branch would leave this RED — which is what this case exists to catch. `the utilities provider` is also the more ordinary English of the two.

cases.trap: the second denylist entry with the same morphology, so the fix cannot be one word
cases.text: During our marriage the provider of renewable energies handled our archive.

observedAtFreeze.promotedBy: relational role term “marriage” within 8 tokens, same clause

cases.note: The denylist was enumerated rather than guessed at: of its sixteen entries, exactly two have a real plural the literal-plus-s test cannot produce, and they are `utility` and `energy`. This is the other one. A patch that special-cases the word in Sol's repro passes cm-16 and fails here.

cases.trap: a plural the stemmer SEPARATES from its singular
cases.text: During our marriage the financial services provider handled our archive.
cases.note: GUARD, green at freeze, and the one that says what the fix is NOT. Stemming is not a superset of the literal-plus-s test it is replacing: `utility` and `utilities` both stem to `utility`, but `service` stems to itself while `services` stems to `servic`, and the same is true of healthcare, insurance, software, care and childcare — eight of the sixteen entries. A fix that swaps literal matching out for stemming rather than adding it turns this case, and cm-03, RED.

cases.trap: a word with the disqualifying MORPHOLOGY and none of the disqualifying sense
cases.text: During our marriage the provider for our families was always him.

observedAtFreeze.promotedBy: relational role term “marriage” within 8 tokens, same clause

cases.note: GUARD, green at freeze. `families` is a y-to-ies plural sitting in exactly the complement slot cm-16's `utilities` sits in, and it is on no list, so it must not disqualify anything. This is the case a fix reaching for a spelling rule — treat any `ies` word as its `y` singular and compare loosely — would break. The denylist, and not the shape of the word, is still what disqualifies.

documentedLimits.question: Which of Sol's failures are the clause model being asked for something punctuation cannot tell it, and what exactly does each one cost?
documentedLimits.ruling: These fifteen. Every one is frozen ASSERTING CURRENT BEHAVIOR, with the humanly correct answer recorded beside it, because that is the difference between a limit and a defect nobody got to. Each names the syntax that defeats the approximation: coordination, subordination, appositives and relatives, attribution chains, quotation ownership, and a token window with a hard edge. None is fixed here and none should be fixed by widening a cue list — the honest fix for most of them is a parser, which is a decision about what this instrument is, not a patch. Until that decision is made, a production flag landing on one of these accumulates in md/limit-hit-ledger.md as the evidence for it.
documentedLimits.misreading: a large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates

cases.text: A large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates even though no guarantee of marriage follows.
cases.note: The source asserts the equivalence; `no` negates only a separate consequence inside a subordinate clause. There is no punctuation, so parity counts a negator that belongs to a different proposition. Representing this needs subordinator scope, which is grammar.

cases.text: It is false that "a large inbox" means this: "a large pool of relationship candidates".
cases.note: An explicit denial of the misreading, split across a colon. The assertion clause is chosen by highest overlap and lands on the second half, which is the fragment without the governing `false`. Sibling of cm-12, which is the unquoted form of the same defeat.

cases.text: The poster equated "a large inbox" with "a large pool of relationship candidates".
cases.note: The equivalence is attributed to the poster by the reporting verb `equated`, which joins two quoted arguments neither of which carries a finite verb. The finite-verb test is what protects sc-07 (irony) from sc-02, so relaxing it here would move a different documented limit.

cases.text: The label read "a large inbox is noisy"; a large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates.
cases.note: Ownership theft. `quotedSpans` is passage-global, so an unrelated quoted proposition — which does carry a finite verb and does share two misreading tokens — is credited with reporting a claim asserted flatly in the next clause. Fixing this means linking a span to the selected occurrence, not to the passage.

cases.text: Alice says Bob claims a large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates.
cases.note: A two-level attribution chain with no speaker endorsement at either level. REPORTED_SPEECH_CUES recognises pronoun and listed-source subjects, not arbitrary named speakers, and adding a name pattern would make every capitalised subject an attribution.

cases.text: A large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates, but the dashboard is too simplistic.
cases.note: The equivalence is asserted flatly; what is called simplistic is the dashboard. QUALIFICATION_CUES is not subject-linked, and linking it requires knowing what the following clause is ABOUT — the same information bl-01 needs, from the other direction.

cases.text: Although that equivalence is overstated, a large inbox is a large pool of relationship candidates.
cases.note: An explicit PRE-posed concession. Follow-up cues are matched only after the assertion, because endorsement and rejection are anaphoric — `that is false` points backwards. Named as an open limitation in v2.5.0 §7.5 before Sol found it independently, which is the useful confirmation: the release predicted its own failure and the review reproduced it.

cases.text: We discussed marriage and the AWS provider failed again.

observedAtFreeze.promotedBy: relational role term “marriage” within 8 tokens, same clause

cases.note: Two coordinated predicates with different subjects and no punctuation between them. bl-15 is the same sentence with a comma before `and`, and it correctly finds nothing — which is Sol's point exactly: this is a punctuation cliff, not semantic discrimination.

cases.text: During our marriage the AWS provider recommended by my wife handled payroll.

observedAtFreeze.promotedBy: relational role term “marriage” within 8 tokens, same clause

cases.note: AWS and payroll establish the technical sense unmistakably, and the relational words are incidental context in a reduced relative clause. `AWS` is not on the denylist and should not be — v2.5.0 §1.2 is right that enumerating vendors is not a rule — and it sits BEFORE the alias, so the v2.6.0 post-nominal fix does not reach it either.

cases.text: During our marriage the provider my husband uses handles payroll.
cases.note: A reduced relative with no complementizer at all — `my husband uses` identifies a technical provider, and the husband is its USER rather than evidence that the word denotes his relational role. The v2.6.0 complement rule requires `for` or `of` immediately after the alias, and there is none, which is the price of keeping that rule narrow enough for cm-04.

cases.text: Throughout their marriage he endured layoffs and setbacks before becoming the provider.
cases.note: The window's hard edge, stated as a number: `marriage` is nine tokens away. bl-11b is the SAME SENTENCE with the article removed, putting it at eight, and it promotes at 0.540. A token radius has to have an edge somewhere and this is where it is; what the pair freezes is that the edge is arithmetic, not meaning.

cases.text: Throughout their marriage he endured layoffs and setbacks before becoming provider.
cases.note: GUARD, and the other half of bl-11. One word of difference, no difference in meaning, opposite verdicts.

cases.text: He was the provider; his wife relied on his income throughout their marriage.
cases.note: The second clause resolves exactly what `provider` means, and clause-clipping is what stops it counting. This is the cost side of the v2.5.0 cf-05/cf-06 pair, which is the benefit side: the same rule that stops a billing vendor borrowing a relational clause stops a relational clause vouching for a genuine one.

cases.text: She wanted a provider, namely her husband, to support their household.
cases.note: A comma-delimited appositive naming the provider as her husband — about as direct as this evidence gets — and the comma that makes it an appositive is the comma that puts it in another clause.

cases.text: She wanted a provider, who would support her future children.
cases.note: A non-restrictive relative clause, clipped for the same reason as bl-13. An appositive and a relative modify the noun they follow; the splitter treats the comma before them as a boundary because that is what a comma usually is.

cases.text: We discussed marriage, and the AWS provider failed again.
cases.note: GUARD, and the measurement that turns bl-08 from an opinion into a finding. One comma separates a right answer from a wrong one on identical content.
